# A bipartisan path to a stronger American grid


By Heather Zichal, Head of Center for Energy and the Environment and Global Head of Sustainability


November 17, 2026

If Alexander Graham Bell returned today, he wouldn't recognize the telecommunications system he helped create. But if Thomas Edison returned, he'd feel right at home with America's electric grid. That's how little we've fundamentally changed the way we deliver electricity in more than a century. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) creates a long-overdue opportunity to modernize how we build, plan and use the electric grid.


An outdated system is putting us at risk. Access to power is at the foundation of the sectors most critical for U.S. competitiveness and national security – like defense, AI and quantum computing, and manufacturing. Meeting their needs will require an estimated $1 trillion of grid investment through 2035.1 Yet under the current system, new power generation and transmission infrastructure can take years to connect, permit, and build, making it harder for our infrastructure to keep pace with growing demand.


JPMorganChase supports BAAJA because it makes necessary reforms to streamline permitting, help lower the cost of capital and facilitate the building of the energy infrastructure America needs. Just as importantly, the bill includes reforms to how we plan, expand, and use the grid, helping us get more out of the infrastructure we have today while building what we need for tomorrow.


## Expand transmission infrastructure


Transmission lines move electricity from where it is generated to where it is needed. When more of them are in operation, they can do this more efficiently, helping lower costs and strengthen reliability. A recent study by CERA Consulting, the consulting arm of S&P Global Energy, found that an expanded interregional transmission network could save electricity customers up to $15.3 billion by 2035.2


But construction has slowed dramatically: the U.S. added just 392 miles of high-voltage transmission lines per year from 2022 to 2025, while the Department of Energy has estimated that roughly 5,000 miles of new high-capacity lines may be needed annually to support future demand.


Electricity does not stop at a regional boundary. Transmission projects can span multiple states and grid regions, requiring different authorities to make decisions about whether and where lines should be built, who benefits, and who should pay. This fragmented approach can make interregional projects particularly difficult to advance.


BAAJA would require neighboring grid operators to plan across those boundaries using common assumptions and criteria for evaluating a project’s benefits. It would also provide a clearer basis for determining who should bear the costs and who stands to benefit.


That could give high-value projects a clearer path to construction, helping deliver affordable power where it is needed and strengthening reliability and resilience across the grid.


## Get more from the grid we already have


Building new transmission is necessary for continued economic growth, but new high-voltage lines are expensive and can take years to plan, permit, and construct. Advanced transmission technologies (ATTs) are hardware and software upgrades that can increase the capacity and efficiency of existing infrastructure. These include replacing existing lines with higher-capacity lines and adding cost-effective technologies that help grid operators better manage how power flows. Because they make better use of existing assets, ATTs can be deployed quickly and add capacity at 5-10 times lower cost than building a new line, which can ultimately improve energy affordability for ratepayers.3


BAAJA would make it easier to upgrade transmission lines in existing rights-of-way and require transmission owners to deploy ATTs when their benefits justify their costs. These upgrades are not substitutes for new lines, but they offer a practical way to unlock additional capacity more quickly and affordably as we do the longer-term work of expanding the grid.


## Plan the grid for the demand of the future


Meeting growing power demand also requires changing how we plan the grid. Today, planning for new transmission and connecting new power generation largely happens through separate processes. That disconnect makes grid investment more reactive and can leave developers uncertain about where projects can connect and what upgrades will be required as a result.4


BAAJA would consolidate generation and transmission planning by requiring grid planners to identify locations where new supply could connect and provide standardized and clear information on interconnection costs upfront. This would give developers and investors greater visibility into where projects can be built, while helping grid planners anticipate future demand instead of continually playing catch-up.


A grid that is planned more efficiently can help shorten interconnection queue delays, deliver projects more efficiently, and decrease the costs of delay that make the electricity system more expensive than it needs to be. These reforms could also support additional clean energy generation—modeling of four regional power systems found that consolidated interconnection planning could enable 65% more battery storage capacity by 2035, alongside 22% more solar and 14% more wind generation.5


Permitting reform is fundamental to building the energy infrastructure America needs, but BAAJA’s vision for the grid goes further. By improving how we expand, use, and plan the grid, the bill would help make our power system more affordable, reliable, and capable of supporting future growth. The goal should be simple: our grid shouldn't be a constraint on American growth. It should be the foundation that enables it.
